chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim, from Ja'far, from his father, from Ali (peace be upon him)
That he disliked the sale of a debt note of silver until it is taken possession of.

key_terms.صَكِّ الْوَرِقِ: Debt note of silver; a written instrument acknowledging a debt payable in silver currency.
key_terms.كَرِهَ: He disliked; indicating a preference for avoiding the act, often implying it is not strictly invalid but less preferred or potentially problematic depending on the school.
key_terms.يُقْبَضَ: To be taken possession of; referring to the physical or constructive transfer of the item or debt.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on selling a debt note (sakk) before receiving possession in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) narrates from his father, and then from Imam Ali (peace be upon him), that he disliked (كره) the sale of a 'sakk al-waraq' (a written debt instrument or promissory note of silver) before actual possession (qabd) is taken. This establishes a ruling on the validity of selling debt instruments in Islamic jurisprudence, specifically reflecting the principle of *bay' al-dayn* (sale of debt) where the underlying asset is silver (*warq*), requiring physical or constructive possession to avoid *riba* (usury) and *gharar* (uncertainty). The ruling underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on ensuring the transfer of ownership is complete and tangible before trading the debt itself, a nuance critical in classical fiqh debates regarding commercial transactions.
